read: partial: abstract, introduction, related work, Section 3 (data creation, validation and expert review), Section 4 (ChainEval), Section 5 (models, ChainEval validation, setup, results by model, domain and difficulty, error analysis), conclusion, limitations, ethics and acknowledgments (pp. 1-9) in full; Appendices A.1, A.3, A.4, B.1-B.6, C, D.1-D.5, E.1-E.3 and F.1 (pp. 13-24) read; the template code examples (pp. 13-15) skimmed
venue_now: ACL 2026 Long Papers, pp. 14529-14553 (papers.json). The fetched text is arXiv:2506.02515v4, 30 Apr 2026 (p. 1); it shows no venue header but thanks anonymous reviewers (p. 9)
what_it_is: A symbolic benchmark for verifiable chain-of-thought financial reasoning. Following GSM-Symbolic, each of 58 topics in 12 financial domains is instantiated by five parameterized templates (two basic, two intermediate, one advanced), each an executable Python program that generates the question, a gold step-by-step solution and the final answer (pp. 1-4, 13). Templates were generated with LLM assistance, checked against validation constraints and reviewed by financial experts; 29 of 290 were found incorrect and revised (pp. 4, 15, 17). Ten instances per template give 2,900 test cases (p. 6). Models are scored with ChainEval, which aligns the predicted steps to the gold trace by dynamic time warping over sentence-embedding similarity gated by a 5% match of intermediate values, plus final-answer correctness at weight 0.1 (pp. 4-5); 26 LLMs are evaluated (pp. 5-6).
size: 290 templates (116 basic, 116 intermediate, 58 advanced; mean 2.01, 2.97 and 3.90 steps; p. 4); 10 instances per template, 2,900 test cases (p. 6); 26 LLMs in four groups: frontier proprietary, finance-specific, math-enhanced, general open-weight (p. 5)
source_of_items: generated from templates: topics proposed with LLM assistance and curated with financial experts; templates generated with LLM assistance and curated by domain experts (pp. 3-4, 13)
instances: generated: instantiated from the template programs with distinct random seeds (p. 6)
has_gold_traces: yes: each instance has an executable gold chain of reasoning, with intermediate values, produced by the template code (pp. 2-3, 13)
evaluation: step-level or process: ChainEval = 0.9 x DTWGate (DTW alignment of predicted to gold steps, each pair scored by sentence-encoder cosine similarity times an indicator that the step's value is within 5% relative error) + 0.1 x FAC (final answer within 5%) (pp. 4-5). Steps and final answers are extracted by regular expressions or GPT-4.1 (pp. 6-7, 21-22). ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L and BERTScore are also reported (p. 6)
human_validation: Templates: ten financial experts (seven graduate students, three industry professionals); 20 templates were reviewed by all in a calibration pilot, after which all agreed; each of the other 270 was reviewed by one expert; 29 of 290 (10%) were found incorrect and revised (pp. 15, 17). Evaluator: 20 questions x 5 models = 100 responses rated 1-5 by financial experts for reasoning-process quality and final-answer accuracy (pp. 5-6, 17-18); ChainEval's Spearman correlation with the process ratings is 0.655 (Pearson 0.584, Kendall 0.509), against 0.469 for ROUGE-2, 0.434 for ROUGE-L and 0.287 for BERTScore (pp. 20-21). The weight alpha = 0.1 and the tolerance epsilon = 0.05 were chosen to maximise that correlation, and no held-out split is reported (pp. 5, 20-21); neither the number of raters per response nor inter-rater agreement is reported. Error analysis on 200 questions with expert-checked labels (p. 8)
contamination_measures: generated instances, described as 'contamination-free' (pp. 1-2, 9); no contamination test is reported, and the templates and code are public on GitHub under the MIT licence (pp. 1, 9)

engtrace_use.sentence: S-I2 (L84-94): 'Symbolic templates (Mirzadeh et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2025) serve as the generative mechanism, producing unique, contamination-resistant instances', which directly follows 'yet no existing benchmark verifies this process. We introduce EngTrace: a symbolic benchmark pairing each problem instance with a gold-standard reasoning trace to enable verifiable process supervision' (L77-84). It is FinChain's only citation in the paper (citation map, Part A, row 70).
engtrace_use.explanation: The literal claim is accurate: FinChain instantiates problems from parameterized symbolic templates 'Following Mirzadeh et al. (2025)' (p. 3), samples instances with distinct seeds (p. 6) and claims contamination-free generation (pp. 1-2, 9); the May paper's 'contamination-resistant' is the more defensible word. But the sentence cites FinChain only for the generative mechanism while presenting as EngTrace's contribution exactly what FinChain already does in finance: it pairs every instance with an explicit, executable gold reasoning trace (p. 2) and scores step-level consistency against that trace with an expert-validated metric (pp. 4-6). The neighbouring claim that 'no existing benchmark verifies this process' is scoped to engineering (L77-80), so FinChain does not contradict it; but leaving out FinChain's gold traces and step-level metric omits what matters most for the comparison, which is the protocol's definition of misleading. A reviewer who knows FinChain will ask what EngTrace adds beyond the domain (citation map D.3, note 1).

suggested_wording: Closest to EngTrace is FinChain (Xie et al., 2025), which generates finance problems from symbolic templates whose executable code also produces a gold chain of reasoning, and scores a model's steps by their alignment to that chain (ChainEval), a metric that correlates with expert ratings of the reasoning (Spearman 0.655 on 100 responses).
facts_to_cite: 58 topics in 12 financial domains, with five templates per topic (two basic, two intermediate, one advanced): 290 templates in all (pp. 2-4).
Templates are executable Python programs that generate the question, the intermediate steps and the final answer, following GSM-Symbolic (pp. 2-3, 13).
10 instances per template give 2,900 test cases (p. 6).

ChainEval aligns predicted to gold steps by dynamic time warping, scoring each step pair by semantic similarity gated by a 5% relative match of intermediate values, and adds final-answer correctness at weight 0.1 (pp. 4-5).
On 100 expert-rated responses, ChainEval's Spearman correlation with reasoning-process ratings is 0.655, against 0.469 for ROUGE-2 and 0.287 for BERTScore (pp. 5-6, 20).
Templates were reviewed by ten financial experts, one expert per template after a 20-template calibration; 29 of 290 were revised (pp. 15, 17).
26 LLMs are evaluated, including finance-specific and math-enhanced models (p. 5); correct final answers do not always come with faithful intermediate steps (p. 7).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares nearly the whole design: symbolic templates with executable gold traces, generated instances, three difficulty tiers in a 2:2:1 template ratio, LLM-assisted template writing with expert review, step-level evaluation, and validation of the metric against expert ratings (pp. 2-6, 15). What EngTrace can say it adds beyond engineering and physical units (EngTrace facts from engtrace_state_brief.md): (1) it checks the trace's own numbers instead of aligning it to the gold step sequence: order-free milestone values at 0.5% tolerance, recomputation of every displayed claim by the digit rule, a residual LLM judge only where the deterministic checks miss, and an answer tolerance of 0.2% relative or one unit of the last digit, against ChainEval's 5% tolerance and embedding-based alignment (pp. 4-5); (2) its evaluator is validated by three own-branch experts per trace on 300 traces, with step-, milestone- and answer-level labels, Fleiss kappa, F1 and AUROC with template-clustered intervals, and planted defects, against a single correlation on 100 responses with alpha and epsilon tuned on the same ratings (pp. 5-6, 20-21); (3) every template is certified by three own-branch experts who each solve an instance by hand, with planted defects, against one expert per template (p. 15), subject to the certification caveats in the state brief, section 1 (the Markdown view that dropped symbols; the disputed round-1 account of the 60 new templates); (4) a private seed with a hashed pool and a paraphrase test of wording memorisation, against public templates and an untested 'contamination-free' claim (pp. 1, 9); (5) six answer types, including multipart, vector and symbolic, against a single target per template (p. 15). EngTrace should not claim expert-written templates as a difference: FinChain's are LLM-generated and expert-curated (p. 4), and per the state brief so are EngTrace's 60 new ones.
notes: The people overlap is wider than the citation map's four shared authors (Xie, Zhang, Stoyanov, Nakov): FinChain's acknowledgments thank 'student volunteers, Muhammad Usman Safder and Ayesha Gull' for its live demo and website (p. 9), and they are EngTrace's first two authors, so six of the seven May authors are connected to FinChain. Under ARR anonymity it has to be cited in the third person, and the differences stated explicitly. The May reference gives no arXiv id or venue: it is arXiv:2506.02515, now ACL 2026 (papers.json). The fetched text is v4 (30 Apr 2026), and the May authors may have read an earlier version. The May paper's design closely parallels FinChain's: a 2:2:1 template split by difficulty (p. 3); 26 models including a math-enhanced group (p. 5), against the May paper's 27 in frontier, open-weights and math-enhanced groups; a metric validated by correlation with experts against ROUGE and BERTScore (p. 20), against the May paper's rho = 0.632 versus 0.325; and a Streamlit annotation platform (p. 15). Two small inconsistencies in FinChain: its template-generation prompt asks for 10 templates per task (p. 13), while the benchmark keeps five per topic (p. 3); and on Kendall tau the top metric is DTW Precision (Gate), 0.511, not ChainEval, 0.509 (p. 21).
